modules.description: Build a reliable coordinate space for every fragment and learn how resolution shapes the image.

lessons.conceptLede: Understand how raw pixels become stable coordinates you can reuse across every screen size.
lessons.intro: Fragment shaders run once per pixel. Before drawing shapes, turn each pixel position into a predictable coordinate you can reason about.

sections.body: gl_FragCoord.xy contains the current pixel position in framebuffer pixels. Its values depend on the viewport, so a 1080-pixel-wide screen produces very different numbers from a 390-pixel-wide phone.
sections.title: Start with the current fragment

sections.body: Divide the fragment coordinate by resolution.xy to convert both axes into a portable 0-to-1 range. This normalized vector is conventionally named uv or st.
sections.title: Normalize once, use everywhere

sections.body: Pixel space is useful for exact sizes. Centered space makes symmetry natural. Aspect-aware space keeps distance-based shapes circular instead of stretching with the screen.
sections.title: Choose coordinates for the job

lessons.takeaway: The center of normalized UV space is always (0.5, 0.5). After centering it becomes (0.0, 0.0). Correct the x-axis before measuring distance so circles remain circular.
lessons.title: Coordinate Systems & UV Space

lessons.conceptLede: Learn how fragment output combines channels, opacity, and interpolation into visible color.
lessons.intro: A fragment shader returns one color for every pixel. Learn how RGB channels, alpha, and color mixing turn numbers into an image.

sections.body: A color is data. Red, green, and blue are three independent values, usually between 0.0 and 1.0. Changing one channel changes one ingredient of the final pixel.
sections.title: Think in channels

sections.body: Feeding uv.x into red and uv.y into green makes position visible. This is a useful debugging technique: gradients reveal whether your coordinates point in the direction and range you expect.
sections.title: Turn coordinates into color

sections.body: mix(a, b, t) blends from color a to color b. At t = 0 you get a, at t = 1 you get b, and every value between creates a smooth transition.
sections.title: Interpolate with mix

lessons.takeaway: vec3 stores red, green, and blue. vec4 adds alpha. Use coordinate-driven gradients to inspect your UVs, then mix colors to build intentional palettes.
lessons.title: Colors & Fragment Output

lessons.conceptLede: Connect app state to GLSL and create animation from elapsed seconds.
lessons.intro: Uniforms let the app send shared values into every fragment. Use elapsed time to create smooth, frame-rate-independent motion.

sections.body: A uniform is a read-only value supplied by the app to every fragment invocation. Resolution, pointer position, and elapsed time are common uniforms because they describe shared frame state.
sections.title: Uniforms connect host and shader

sections.body: u_time usually stores seconds since the animation started. Feeding it into sin creates smooth repeating motion without counting frames or depending on a particular refresh rate.
sections.title: Animate with elapsed time

sections.body: Multiply time before using it: 0.5 runs at half speed and 2.0 runs twice as fast. The animation remains frame-rate independent because its position comes from elapsed time, not frame count.
sections.title: Control speed with multiplication

lessons.takeaway: Uniforms are shared inputs, not per-pixel variables. Derive motion from elapsed seconds, then multiply time to control speed without tying animation to frame rate.
lessons.title: Uniforms & Time

lessons.conceptLede: Apply translation, scale, rotation, and repetition to UVs before evaluating a reusable shape.
lessons.conceptTitle: Move the space, not the shape
lessons.intro: Transforming UVs lets you position, resize, rotate, and repeat a shape without changing the shape function itself.

sections.body: A shader has no movable object to transform. Instead, subtract an offset from the coordinates before evaluating the shape. Moving the coordinate system left makes the rendered shape appear to move right.
sections.title: Move the coordinate system

sections.body: Multiplying coordinates changes how quickly distance grows, so larger coordinate values make a shape appear smaller. Rotation matrices turn coordinates around the origin, which is why centering UVs first matters.
sections.title: Scale and rotate around the origin

sections.body: fract keeps only the fractional part of each coordinate. Scale first and fract folds the plane into repeating cells—one shape function can then draw an entire pattern.
sections.title: Repeat space with fract

lessons.takeaway: Transform coordinates before drawing. Center them before scaling or rotation, remember that coordinate transforms feel inverse to object transforms, and use fract to fold space into repeatable cells.
lessons.title: Transforming UVs

lessons.conceptLede: Deconstruct a finished shader into coordinate, mask, motion, and color layers.
lessons.intro: Combine coordinates, color, time, and transforms into one layered composition. Isolate each ingredient, then study how they work together.

sections.body: Start with a moving grid, then create rings and an orbiting point as separate masks. Small, testable layers make a complex shader easier to reason about than one long expression.
sections.title: Build from independent layers

sections.body: Normalize, center, and correct aspect ratio once. Every layer then agrees about the origin and distance, so circles stay round and the composition behaves consistently across screens.
sections.title: Reuse one coordinate foundation

sections.body: Use mix to assign each mask a palette role, then combine the layers in a deliberate order. Your checkpoint: identify the coordinate, color, time, and transform idea responsible for every visible part.
sections.title: Compose masks with intention

lessons.takeaway: Complex shaders are compositions of simple masks. Build and inspect each layer independently, share one aspect-correct coordinate system, then combine colors in a deliberate order.
lessons.title: Foundation Challenge
lessons.tryHint: Inspect one layer at a time

modules.title: Coordinate Foundations

modules.description: Turn distance fields into clean geometric forms with thresholds, smooth edges, and composition.

lessons.conceptLede: A shape appears when a distance field crosses a threshold.
lessons.intro: Threshold functions turn continuous measurements into visible boundaries. Compare a hard decision with a controllable, anti-aliased transition.

sections.body: A distance field stores how far each fragment is from a boundary. Negative values are inside, zero is exactly on the edge, and positive values are outside. Keeping this measurement continuous makes the same field reusable.
sections.title: Measure before deciding

sections.body: step(edge, value) returns 0 below the threshold and 1 at or above it. It is ideal for logical masks, but a one-pixel transition can shimmer or look jagged when the shape moves.
sections.title: step makes a binary choice

sections.body: smoothstep blends between two thresholds with a smooth curve. Place those thresholds on either side of zero to create a controlled anti-aliased boundary without changing the underlying shape.
sections.title: smoothstep gives the edge width

lessons.takeaway: Keep distance and visibility separate: first calculate d, then convert d into a fill, outline, or soft edge. One distance field can support many visual treatments.
lessons.title: Step & Smoothstep
lessons.tryHint: Compare four ways to reveal a distance

lessons.conceptLede: Small functions turn coordinates into scalable, composable geometry.
lessons.intro: Signed distance functions describe reusable geometric primitives. Build circles, boxes, and rounded rectangles from compact mathematical measurements.

codeLines: vec3 color = cyan * circle + lime * box;
presets.label: Combined

sections.body: length(p) measures radial distance from the origin. Subtracting a radius moves the zero boundary outward, producing a signed field that is negative inside the circle.
sections.title: Circles come from length

sections.body: A box begins with abs(p), which mirrors all quadrants into one. Subtract the half-size, measure positive overflow outside the corners, and preserve the largest negative component inside.
sections.title: Boxes measure each axis

sections.body: Evaluate a slightly smaller box and subtract a radius from its distance. The zero boundary expands evenly around the corners, turning the sharp box into a rounded rectangle.
sections.title: Radius modifies the field

lessons.takeaway: Write primitives as functions that return signed distance, not color. That keeps size, position, edge treatment, and later boolean operations independent.
lessons.title: Circles & Boxes
lessons.tryHint: Swap the primitive while keeping the edge code

lessons.conceptLede: Boolean-looking operations emerge directly from distance fields.
lessons.intro: Signed distances can be combined like solid geometry. Use min and max to unite, intersect, subtract, and compare shapes without branches.

sections.body: At every fragment, min(a, b) selects whichever shape has the smaller signed distance. If either field is negative, the union is inside, so both silhouettes become one field.
sections.title: Union keeps the nearer field

sections.body: max(a, b) is negative only when both inputs are negative. It therefore preserves the overlap and discards areas belonging to just one shape.
sections.title: Intersection keeps shared interior

sections.body: Negating b turns its interior positive. max(a, -b) retains shape a except where b cuts into it. More elaborate expressions produce exclusive regions and reusable cutouts.
sections.title: Negation flips inside and outside

lessons.takeaway: For signed fields: min unites, max intersects, and negating a field swaps inside with outside. Combine distances first and apply smoothstep only once at the final boundary.
lessons.title: Boolean Shape Operations
lessons.tryHint: Apply four operations to the same two fields

lessons.conceptLede: Coordinate folding replaces duplicated drawing code.
lessons.intro: Repeat coordinate space before evaluating a primitive, then layer multiple masks and transformations into patterns that remain compact and controllable.

sections.body: Scale normalized coordinates, apply fract, and subtract 0.5. Every fragment is now expressed relative to the center of a repeating cell, so one primitive appears many times.
sections.title: Fold space into cells

sections.body: floor before fract gives each cell an integer ID. Use that ID to alternate color, rotation, scale, or timing while still evaluating one shared shape function.
sections.title: Preserve the cell identity

sections.body: Keep repeated circles and boxes as separate masks until color composition. Independent layers are easier to tune and can later become inputs to boolean distance operations.
sections.title: Layer masks intentionally

lessons.takeaway: Repeat coordinates, not drawing calls. Keep local cell coordinates and integer cell IDs so geometry stays reusable while variation remains deterministic.
lessons.title: Repetition & Composition
lessons.tryHint: Build complexity from a single repeated cell

lessons.conceptLede: Complex icons are deliberate compositions of simple fields.
lessons.intro: Combine edges, primitives, boolean operations, repetition, and motion into recognizable procedural marks built entirely from distance fields.

codeLines: color = violet * head + lime * max(eyes, mouth);
presets.label: Face

codeLines: color = cyan * fill(symbol) + violet * fill(cut) + lime * frame;
presets.label: Final mark

sections.body: Choose a small vocabulary: one outer frame, one dominant filled form, and one contrasting cutout or detail. Assign each element a distance field before thinking about color.
sections.title: Start from a visual brief

sections.body: Identify where the composition uses a threshold, primitive, union, intersection, subtraction, repetition, or transform. If one expression is hard to explain, isolate it as a named intermediate field.
sections.title: Audit every operation

sections.body: Motion should clarify structure. Pulse a radius, rotate repeated cells, or shift an edge width while keeping the underlying mark recognizable and frame-rate independent.
sections.title: Animate a parameter, not the identity

lessons.takeaway: A finished procedural mark is a hierarchy: coordinates feed primitives, primitives combine into one field, the field becomes masks, and masks receive color and motion. Debug the hierarchy one layer at a time.
lessons.title: Shape Synthesis Challenge

modules.title: Shape Synthesis

modules.description: Mix palettes, understand luminance, and shape color with reusable procedural functions.

lessons.conceptLede: mix() interpolates every channel at once; the real design decision is the value you feed into it.
lessons.intro: Color is another signal you can shape with coordinates. Learn to interpolate two or more colors, control the transition curve, and turn spatial measurements into deliberate palettes.

codeLines: vec3 color = mix(left, right, step(0.5, uv.x));
presets.label: Three stops

sections.body: For colors a and b, mix(a, b, t) computes a * (1 - t) + b * t for red, green, and blue independently. A t of 0 returns a, 1 returns b, and values between them trace a straight path through RGB space.
sections.title: Interpolation is channel-wise

sections.body: A raw UV coordinate creates an even gradient. Passing it through smoothstep delays both ends and emphasizes the center transition. Distance, noise, time, or a shape mask can all become t, turning the same two colors into entirely different compositions.
sections.title: Shape the blend factor

sections.body: A multi-stop gradient is several small mixes joined across adjacent ranges. Remap each range back to 0–1 before mixing, then choose its result with a threshold. This keeps every stop intentional and reusable.
sections.title: Build longer palettes in segments

lessons.takeaway: Color mixing becomes procedural when the blend factor comes from the image itself. First choose the endpoints, then design the scalar field that travels between them.
lessons.title: Color Mixing

lessons.conceptLede: A weighted dot product compresses RGB into one useful measurement without treating every channel as equally bright.
lessons.conceptTitle: Read the light inside a color
lessons.intro: Brightness is not the average of red, green, and blue. Convert color to perceptual luma, then use that scalar signal to adjust contrast, isolate value bands, and manage exposure.

sections.body: The Rec. 709 luma weights assign the most influence to green, less to red, and very little to blue. The dot product turns those three weighted contributions into a single brightness estimate you can reuse as a mask or control value.
sections.title: Human vision favors green

sections.body: Subtracting 0.5 moves mid-gray to zero. Scaling then pushes darker values down and brighter values up; adding 0.5 restores the original range. Values may leave 0–1, so clamp when later operations require a bounded signal.
sections.title: Contrast pivots around a midpoint

sections.body: Multiplication brightens linearly and can clip abruptly. The exponential exposure curve rises quickly but approaches white gradually, preserving a softer highlight transition that feels closer to light accumulating on a sensor.
sections.title: Exposure rolls into white

lessons.takeaway: Luma converts color into structure. Once brightness is a scalar field, the same threshold, remapping, and easing tools used for shapes can art-direct the light in an image.
lessons.title: Luma & Contrast
lessons.tryHint: Inspect and reshape the brightness signal

lessons.conceptLede: Four vec3 parameters control the center, range, repetition, and channel timing of an entire gradient.
lessons.intro: A palette can be a function instead of a list. Use offset, amplitude, frequency, and phase to generate smooth families of colors from one scalar input.

codeLines: return a + b * cos(TAU * (c * t + d));
presets.label: Cosine ramp

codeLines: vec3 color = a + b * cos(TAU * (c * uv.x + d));
presets.label: Channel phase

codeLines: vec3 color = a + b * cos(TAU * (c * t + phase));
presets.label: Animated palette

sections.body: Parameter a is the palette's center color, while b controls how far each channel swings above and below it. Starting both near 0.5 tends to keep the result inside displayable 0–1 values.
sections.title: Offset and amplitude set the range

sections.body: Parameter c controls how often each channel cycles as t changes. Parameter d shifts those cycles relative to each other. Separating the red, green, and blue phases produces richer hue travel than moving every channel together.
sections.title: Frequency and phase create character

sections.body: The palette function does not know about pixels. Feed it uv.x for a strip, distance for rings, angle for a wheel, a shape distance for colored edges, or time for motion. The same palette becomes a reusable rendering tool.
sections.title: The input connects palette to form

lessons.takeaway: A procedural palette separates color design from spatial design. Tune the four color parameters once, then reuse the function with any scalar field your shader produces.
lessons.title: Procedural Palettes
lessons.tryHint: Change how one palette function travels through color

lessons.conceptLede: A normal, a light direction, and a few dot products are enough to suggest three-dimensional form in a fragment shader.
lessons.conceptTitle: Make a flat field feel illuminated
lessons.intro: Combine Module 3 into a luminous procedural orb. Build its albedo from a palette, recover a surface normal, add diffuse and rim light, then animate a polished final composition.

codeLines: float orb = 1.0 - smoothstep(r - aa, r + aa, length(p));
presets.label: Palette albedo

sections.body: Inside a circle of radius r, the missing z coordinate of a sphere is sqrt(r² - x² - y²). Combining p.x, p.y, and z produces a normal that turns a flat circle into a surface whose orientation changes across every fragment.
sections.title: Recover a sphere normal

sections.body: Diffuse light measures how directly the surface faces the light. Rim light strengthens edges that turn away from the camera. Specular light compares the surface normal with the halfway direction between the light and viewer, creating a tight highlight.
sections.title: Layer distinct lighting cues

sections.body: Multiplying only by diffuse makes the unlit side perfectly black. A small ambient term preserves the palette in shadow, while a restrained halo connects the bright material to its background without hiding the orb's silhouette.
sections.title: Keep ambient light in the mix

lessons.takeaway: Convincing procedural light is a controlled sum of readable cues. Preserve the base palette, add each lighting term for a reason, and animate the light direction instead of rebuilding the material.
lessons.title: Color & Light Challenge
lessons.tryHint: Assemble the final material one lighting layer at a time
